# Speech and Realtime Voice {#sec-speech}

The diffusion models of @sec-diffusion generate media in pixels; this chapter
handles the other major modality, audio. Speech has its own stack, recognizing it, synthesizing it, and
holding a conversation in it, and its own governing constraint: latency. A live
voice has to reply within a few hundred milliseconds, and that single number
shapes every architectural choice. By the end of this chapter a reader can
explain how audio became a token-modeling problem like everything else in this
book, why a three-second clip is enough to clone a voice, and why a voice agent's
design is decided by its latency budget rather than its components.

## Recognizing speech

Automatic speech recognition maps a waveform to text, and the standard backbone
pairs convolution, which captures local acoustic detail, with self-attention,
which captures long-range structure: the Conformer [@gulati2020conformer]. The
expensive part was always labeled audio, and two ideas drove that cost down.
Self-supervision came first: wav2vec 2.0 pretrains on raw audio by masking the
signal in latent space and solving a contrastive task over quantized latent
representations, then reaches strong recognition from as little as ten minutes of
labels [@baevski2020wav2vec2]. Scale came next: Whisper trained on 680,000 hours
of weakly-supervised multilingual, multitask audio and generalizes zero-shot to
new benchmarks without fine-tuning, approaching human robustness
[@radford2022whisper]. The arc mirrors the text side of the book, self-supervised
pretraining then large weakly-supervised scaling.

## Audio as tokens

The move that folded audio into the rest of this book was to stop treating it as
a continuous signal and start treating it as discrete tokens. A neural codec does
this: an encoder compresses a waveform, a residual vector quantizer maps it to a
short sequence of codebook indices, and a decoder reconstructs it, all trained
end to end. SoundStream at 3 kbps outperforms the traditional Opus codec at 12
kbps [@zeghidour2021soundstream], and EnCodec pushed fidelity further with a
streaming encoder-decoder over a quantized latent space [@defossez2022encodec].
Residual quantization is the key trick: each quantizer codes the leftover the
previous ones missed, so depth trades bitrate against reconstruction error. Once
audio is a token sequence, a language model can model it.

:::: {.runnable}
```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

d, K, Q = 16, 256, 6            # frame dim, codebook size, RVQ depth (num quantizers)
codebooks = [0.5 * rng.normal(size=(K, d)) for _ in range(Q)]
x = rng.normal(size=d)          # one audio-frame embedding to compress

residual = x.copy(); tokens = []
for cb in codebooks:
    j = int(np.argmin(((cb - residual) ** 2).sum(1)))   # nearest entry to residual
    tokens.append(j)
    residual = residual - cb[j]                          # quantize the leftover
    print(f"{len(tokens)} quantizer(s) -> {len(tokens)} token(s), "
          f"recon error = {np.linalg.norm(residual):.3f}")
print("each extra quantizer codes the leftover residual: error falls, bitrate rises")
```
::::

## Generating speech

With audio as tokens, generation becomes language modeling. AudioLM casts audio
generation as predicting the next token over a hierarchy of semantic tokens, from
a self-supervised model, and acoustic tokens, from the codec, producing coherent
speech and even piano continuations with no transcript [@borsos2022audiolm].
Text-to-speech followed the same turn from signal regression to token prediction:
VALL-E treats TTS as conditional codec-language-modeling and, given a
three-second enrollment recording of an unseen speaker, clones the voice
zero-shot, carrying over the speaker's emotion and acoustic environment
[@wang2023valle]. The older pipeline of predicting a mel-spectrogram and running
a separate vocoder gives way to one model emitting codec tokens, the same
consolidation the text stack made.

## Realtime, full-duplex voice

The hard part of a voice agent is not recognition or synthesis but the
conversation loop: turn-taking, interruption, and latency. The obvious design is
a cascade, automatic speech recognition into a text model into text-to-speech.
It is modular and rides text-model progress, but it stacks each stage's latency
and flattens everything through a text bottleneck that discards timing, overlap,
and prosody. The alternative models speech to speech directly. Moshi is a
full-duplex speech-text model that removes explicit speaker turns, models its own
audio and the user's as two parallel streams alongside an "inner monologue" text
stream, and reports about 160 ms of theoretical and 200 ms of practical latency
[@defossez2024moshi]. A parallel line unifies the tasks rather than the duplex
loop: SeamlessM4T is a single model for speech-to-speech, speech-to-text,
text-to-speech, and text-to-text translation plus recognition across roughly a
hundred languages [@seamless2023].

::: {.callout-important}
## What's contested
Whether a voice agent should be a cascade or an end-to-end speech-to-speech model
is unsettled. The cascade is debuggable and inherits every text-model
improvement, but pays serial latency and throws away paralinguistics, the
emotion, overlap, and timing that make speech more than its transcript. The
end-to-end route keeps those and cuts latency, but is harder to train, steer, and
evaluate, and cannot drop in a better text model the way a cascade can. The
choice is set by how much the product values expressiveness and sub-second
response against controllability, not by a general verdict.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Constraint arrow
The latency budget of a conversation reaches back into the architecture. People
expect a reply within roughly a few hundred milliseconds, and that ceiling, not
any accuracy target, is what rules out a serial recognize-then-think-then-speak
cascade for the most demanding cases and forces streaming, token-interleaved,
full-duplex designs that emit audio before the user has finished. The
interaction's latency dictates the model, the way the serving cost of a token
dictates model size in @sec-scaling-laws.
:::
